\section{A degree budget obtained from divisibility}
For $p(x)=\bigoplus_{S\in\mathcal M}x^S$ over $\F_2$, with $|S|\le k$,
form
\begin{equation}\label{eq:binaryproduct}
 F(X,V)=\prod_{S\in\mathcal M}(1-2VX^S)
       \quad\text{in }\Q[V]/(V^{n+2}).
\end{equation}
$V$ is a formal bookkeeping variable, not a Boolean state. Give each
factor independent incidence indeterminates before measuring degree.
A retained term of $V$-degree $j$ selects $j$ nonconstant factor parts,
so its incidence degree is at most $kj$. The full retained product has
degree at most $k(n+1)$, independently of $m$. This satisfies the exact
degree hypothesis of Proposition 3.4 without globally identifying and
multilinearizing all copies.

On Boolean inputs the untruncated product at $V=1$ is $(-1)^{p(x)}$.
Discarded orders $j\ge n+2$ are divisible by $2^{n+2}$. After reconstructing
the retained polynomial at the undeformed point,
\[
 \sum_x\sum_{j=0}^{n+1}[V^j]F(x,V)
 \equiv Z_p:=\sum_x(-1)^{p(x)}\pmod {2^{n+2}}.
\]
Since $Z_p\in[-2^n,2^n]$, centered reconstruction recovers it and
$\#\{x:p(x)=0\}=(2^n+Z_p)/2$. Just $n+1$ modular bits would identify
the endpoints $+2^n$ and $-2^n$.

For general phase tables, multilinearly interpolate
$x\mapsto\zeta^{f_j(x)}$ to $G_j\in\Z[\zeta][X_{I_j}]$, of degree
at most $k$ and with at most $2^k$ coefficients. This costs $O_k(1)$
operations per explicit table. Put $\pi=\zeta-1$. Modulo $(\pi)$ each
table is identically one. Boolean finite differences therefore show
that every coefficient of $G_j-1$ is divisible by $\pi$.

\begin{lemma}[Exact finite filtration]\label{lem:filtration}
Set $P=n+2$, $\ell=dP$, and
\[
 \mathcal A=\Q(\zeta)[V]/(V^\ell),\qquad B_j=1+V(G_j-1).
\]
The retained product $\prod_jB_j$ has incidence degree at most
$K=k(\ell-1)$. Its coefficient sum on Boolean inputs agrees with the
original phase product modulo $2^P\Z[\zeta]$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Count the selected nonconstant parts for the degree bound.
Also $\pi^d\in2\Z[\zeta]$. For $d=1$, $\pi=-2$.
For $d\ge2$, expand $(\zeta-1)^d$: the endpoints cancel since
$\zeta^d=-1$, and all intermediate binomial coefficients are even
because $d$ is a power of two. An omitted term has at least $dP$
factors in $(\pi)$ and hence belongs to $2^P\Z[\zeta]$.
\end{proof}

Use the integral basis $1,\zeta,\ldots,\zeta^{d-1}$, with
$\zeta^d=-1$. Each input contributes one signed basis vector, so every
coordinate of $Z$ lies in $[-2^n,2^n]$. Its residues modulo $2^{n+2}$
determine all coordinates exactly. No ramification unit is needed.

\begin{remark}[A final linear map, not a homomorphism]
Setting $V=1$ is not an algebra homomorphism on the truncated ring.
Sum coefficients in its unique representative of degree below $\ell$
only after exact reconstruction at the undeformed point. The lemma
justifies this final map. The modular congruence is required only at
original Boolean inputs; the non-Boolean, rational replacements at
other points are handled by exact rational arithmetic.
\end{remark}

\section{Finding clean information without knowing the errors}
\label{sec:clean}
\begin{lemma}[An unknown clean-column witness]\label{lem:clean}
Under the promise of Theorem~\ref{thm:acquire}, there are sets
$I,E_0\subseteq[n]$ with $|I|\le r$, $|E_0|\le s_0$, such that
for $R_0=[n]\setminus E_0$,
\[
B[R_0,I]=D[R_0,I],\qquad
\col(D[R_0,R_0])\subseteq\col(B[R_0,I]).
\]
Every column of $(B+D)[R_0,R_0]$ has weight at most $\delta$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
In the hidden error graph let $H=\{i:\deg_S(i)\ge\delta\}$.
Its degree sum is at most $2M$, so
$|H|\le\lfloor2M/\delta\rfloor$. Put $V=[n]\setminus H$.
Choose column indices $I\subseteq V$ forming a basis for
$\col(D[V,V])$; there are at most $r$.
Let $J$ be the union of the $S$-neighbors of $I$ within $V$ and
set $E_0=H\cup J\cup I$. Every vertex in $V$ has error degree
at most $\delta-1$, so $|J\cup I|\le r(\delta-1)+r=r\delta$.
There are no off-diagonal errors between $R_0$ and $I$, and
deleting $I$ removes the unknown diagonal discrepancy from these
columns. Restricting the basis relations on $V$ proves the
column-space inclusion. Remaining off-diagonal errors have
column weight at most $\delta-1$; the unknown diagonal adds
at most one discrepancy per column.
\end{proof}

The basis indices in $I$ may lie in the deleted set; this
construction deliberately deletes them. The algorithm must keep
reading the corresponding \emph{external columns of the original
matrix}. Requiring the basis indices to survive is invalid.
Also the acquired column code may be a proper supercode of the
true retained column space, because principal restriction can
reduce the latter rank. Equality is not required.

\section{Short codewords turn erasures into unique decoding}
\label{sec:prune}
Enumerate all unordered $I\subseteq[n]$ with $|I|\le r$ and
$E_0\subseteq[n]$ with $|E_0|\le s_0$. For each pair, start with
$R=[n]\setminus E_0$ and compute independent generators for
$\mathcal C_R=\col(B[R,I])\subseteq\F_2^R$.
This step sees only $B,I,E_0$ and never accesses the hidden
matrices used in Lemma~\ref{lem:clean}.

\begin{lemma}[Distance by deleting supports]\label{lem:prune}
By deleting at most $2r\delta$ further coordinates, one can make
every nonzero word of the restricted code have weight greater
than $2\delta$. This takes $\poly(n)2^r$ time and polynomial
space. Any sequence of qualifying deletions works.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Enumerate codewords using the current independent generators.
If a nonzero word has weight at most $2\delta$, delete its
support and restrict the generators to the surviving coordinates.
This restriction map has a nonzero kernel, namely the chosen
word, so its code dimension strictly decreases. Recompute a
basis and repeat. There are at most $r$ rounds, each deleting at
most $2\delta$ coordinates. At most $2^r$ words are scanned per
round. Generate them one at a time; storing all words would
violate the polynomial-space claim.
\end{proof}

For the witness in Lemma~\ref{lem:clean}, inclusion of the true
remaining column space in the code survives every restriction.
Each observed remaining column is still within distance $\delta$
of its true column. At termination the code has minimum nonzero
distance greater than $2\delta$, so that true column is its unique
codeword within distance $\delta$.

Decode each column of $B[R,R]$ by scanning the codewords. Reject
if any column has no nearby word. Let $C$ be the decoded matrix.
Independently verify symmetry, rank at most $r$, and that
$S'=B[R,R]+\off(C)$ has at most $M$ unordered edges. The empty
code is allowed; its only word is zero. A wrong seed can fail
these checks or give a different valid representation, but
cannot give a false accepted identity.

The correct witness decodes to $D[R,R]$ and passes. The deletion
bound is $|E|\le\min(n,s_0+2r\delta)=s$.
Each candidate takes $\poly(n)2^r$ time and
polynomial space, including decoding, Gaussian elimination,
and verification. Multiplying by the two unordered-subset counts
proves Theorem~\ref{thm:acquire}. No $2^{\Theta(r^2)}$ search
over inner symmetric coefficient matrices is present.

\section{Universal fibers and optimal Boolean synthesis}
\label{sec:synthesis}
For the acquired scalar coordinate classes $A_1,\ldots,A_d$, set
\[
s_a(y)=\sum_{j\in A_a}y_j\pmod4.
\]
These summaries are linear over $\Z/4\Z$ on the acquired Boolean
coordinates. In the original inputs, first compute the retained
invertible binary coordinate change; they are not claimed to be
$\Z/4\Z$-linear directly in the original bits.
Since $\binom w2\bmod2$ depends only on $w\bmod4$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:summaryquad}
q_{\off(C)}(y)=\sum_aH_{aa}\binom{s_a(y)}2+
\sum_{a<b}H_{ab}(s_a(y)\bmod2)(s_b(y)\bmod2)\pmod2.
\end{equation}
Denote this sign by $h_H(s)$ and put
$F_0(y)=(-1)^{f(y)+q_{S'}(y)}$, including its constant.
The signed local fiber population satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fiber}
W(s):=\sum_{y:s(y)=s}F_0(y)
=4^{-d}\sum_{\chi\in(\Z/4\Z)^d}i^{-\chi\cdot s}T_\chi,
\quad
T_\chi=\sum_yF_0(y)i^{\sum_a\chi_a s_a(y)}.
\end{equation}
Character orthogonality proves this identity. Every $T_\chi$
has the same local factors and only additional unary fourth-root
phases. It is an exactly reconstructible family shared by all
fibers and by any subsequent Boolean function of the summaries.

\begin{theorem}[Exact synthesis within acquired summaries]\label{thm:synth}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:raw} and
\eqref{eq:regime}, conditional on the local-phase theorem,
the exact numbers of zeros and ones of the original $p$ can be
streamed for every summary fiber. One can output a Boolean
predictor minimizing uniform-input mistakes among \emph{all
Boolean functions of these acquired summaries}. The bit time is
\[
\poly(L+n)\left(2^{O(\beta^2)}
+2^{4R+F(n,m_0+e(S')+O(n))}\right),
\]
with polynomial working space and at most $4^R$ output rows.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Compute $a_j(t)=\sum_{w\equiv t\ (4)}\binom{|A_j|}{w}$ by
four-state dynamic programming. The unlabelled fiber size is
$N(s)=\prod_j a_j(s_j)$, because the classes partition all
coordinates. Its original-label imbalance is $h_H(s)W(s)$.
Consequently
\[
N_0(s)=\frac{N(s)+h_H(s)W(s)}2,\qquad
N_1(s)=\frac{N(s)-h_H(s)W(s)}2.
\]
Predict one exactly when $N_1(s)>N_0(s)$, choosing zero on
ties and empty fibers. The independent fiber optima give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:risk}
\operatorname{Err}_{\min}
=\sum_s\min(N_0(s),N_1(s))
=\frac{2^n-\sum_s|W(s)|}{2}.
\end{equation}
There are $4^d$ fibers and $4^d$ characters for each. Recompute
the $T_\chi$ as necessary and output each fiber immediately.
This gives the time and polynomial working space. Each inner
answer is reconstructed exactly before division by $4^d$;
the numerator has $O(n+2d)$ bits. Populations and error totals
have $O(n)$ bits.
\end{proof}

Here $d$ is the number of indicator classes, not merely $\rank C$.
Compacting to an overlapping column basis loses the product
population formula. The possible $4^R$-row output is explicitly
subexponential, not asserted polynomial.
Any specified Boolean program $h$ on the $2d$ bit encodings of
the summaries can also be evaluated against these fibers:
\[
\sum_yF_0(y)(-1)^{h(s(y))}
=\sum_s W(s)(-1)^{h(s)}.
\]
Its description and evaluation cost are charged, without counting
its intermediate states as independent inputs. The theorem is
neither globally optimal compression, unrestricted synthesis,
nor sample-based statistical learning.

\section{Manufacturing and decoding the quadratic code}
\subsection{The code is an output of acquisition}
Let $g_1,\ldots,g_d$ be the binary power basis of the acquired field and $G$ its trace Gram matrix. Each binary matrix block is converted to a linear map $L:F\to F$ by applying $G^{-1}$ to its columns. This is an invertible change of output coordinates and preserves binary rank.

For a compatible block in \eqref{eq:band}, precompose by the invertible Frobenius map:
\[
 f(X)=L(X^{2^s})=\sum_{j=0}^{2s}c_{j-s}X^{2^j}.
\]
The evaluations $(f(g_1),\ldots,f(g_d))$ form a length-$d$, dimension-$k$ Gabidulin code over $F$, where $k=2s+1$. A nonzero linearized polynomial of Frobenius degree at most $k-1$ has at most $2^{k-1}$ roots. Its kernel dimension is at most $k-1$, so its binary rank is at least $d-k+1=d-2s$. This proves the required minimum-distance bound directly; the code and its decoders have established ancestry \cite{silva,bombar}.

Every block of the actual defect $D$ has rank at most $r$, since block extraction is a row and column restriction. Trace-coordinate conversion and Frobenius precomposition preserve that rank. Thus each received block is uniquely decodable at radius
\[
 t=\left\lfloor\frac{d-k}{2}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{d-2s-1}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
The field, evaluation points and code coefficients were all manufactured from the raw tensor. There is no assumed free code decomposition.

\subsection{An explicit deterministic interpolation decoder}
Suppose the received map is $y=f+e$, with $\deg_2 f<k$ and $\rank e\le t$. Here $\deg_2$ is the largest index in a linearized polynomial, not its ordinary degree. Solve for a monic $E$ and $N$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{eq:decoder}
 E(y(g_j))=N(g_j)\quad(1\le j\le d),\qquad
 \deg_2 E=t,\quad \deg_2N<k+t.
\end{equation}
Writing $E(X)=X^{2^t}+\sum_{i<t}e_iX^{2^i}$ makes this a linear system over $F$ in $k+2t\le d$ unknown coefficients.

There is a solution. The image of $e$ is a binary subspace of dimension $u\le t$ and has a monic linearized annihilator of Frobenius degree $u$. Composing with enough squarings gives a monic annihilator of degree $t$. Choose $N=E\circ f$.

Every solution of \eqref{eq:decoder} works. The polynomial $H=N-E\circ f$ vanishes on $\ker e$, whose dimension is at least $d-t$. But $\deg_2 H\le k+t-1<d-t$. The root bound forces $H=0$. Recover $f$ by composition division with $E$ on the left: from a leading coefficient $c$ at index $t+j$, recover the next coefficient $a$ by $a^{2^t}=c$, subtract $E\circ(aX^{2^j})$, and continue. Frobenius is invertible, so this step is exact and polynomial-time. Finally verify zero remainder and rank distance at most $t$.

This is the established left-annihilator decoding formulation; confusing it with a right-hand interpolation system would incorrectly assert extension-field linearity. The implementation and an independent audit both check the orientation. Errors may be adversarial and may have rank strictly less than the chosen maximal radius.

There are $b^2$ blocks. Their interpolation systems have at most $d$ rows and unknowns over a degree-$d$ binary field. Ordinary Gaussian elimination uses $O(b^2d^3)$ field operations. With classical binary polynomial arithmetic this is polynomial bit cost, for example $O(b^2d^5)$ for the dominant multiplications. Undo Frobenius, reassemble $B_0$, verify symmetry and zero diagonal, and compute the exact rank of $D=B+B_0$. Under the promise the planted matrices are recovered. Outside it, only a verified identity is accepted.

\section{Integrating the decoded blocks and reconstructing counts}
\subsection{A polynomial of bounded ordinary degree is constructed}
For $i<j$, a positive-index block term gives
\[
 \Tr(c_aX_iX_j^{2^a}),\qquad 0\le a\le s.
\]
A negative-index term is folded without increasing the promised degree beyond $2^s+1$:
\[
 \Tr(c_{-a}X_iX_j^{2^{-a}})
 =\Tr(c_{-a}^{2^a}X_i^{2^a}X_j),\qquad 1\le a\le s.
\]
For a diagonal block, self-adjointness of $L$ imposes
\[
 c_{-a}=c_a^{2^{d-a}}.
\]
These paired terms contribute zero to $\Tr(XL(X))$. Alternation therefore forces $c_0=0$. The quadratic refinement
\[
 Q_i(X_i)=\Tr\left(\sum_{a=1}^{s}c_aX_i^{1+2^a}\right)
\]
has exactly the required diagonal polar form. The strict inequality $2s<d$ keeps every positive and negative index distinct.

The refinement need not equal the canonical binary quadratic: its values on individual binary basis vectors may be nonzero. Correct this with a Boolean linear function, represented uniquely by a field-trace linear form through $G^{-1}$. More generally, after adding the canonical cubic $C$, match the raw values at zero and at all binary basis vectors. This supplies all remaining affine terms. For a constant one, choose an acquired field element of trace one; taking the field element $1$ is wrong when $d$ is even.

The resulting field polynomial $P_0$ has ordinary degree at most $D_s=2^s+1$. It uses $O(b^3+b^2s)$ sparse monomials. With its coordinate matrix and a rank factorization of the defect, the representation occupies
\[
 O\bigl(n^2+nr+d(b^3+b^2s)\bigr)
\]
bits up to ordinary index-encoding factors. This is manufactured from the raw coefficient list. Equality follows from equality of the third tensor, quadratic polar form and affine part. Alternatively, every constructed trace monomial has Boolean degree at most three, so checking all coefficients by evaluations at Hamming weights at most three is a polynomial-size global identity test.

The family is invariant under affine changes of its $b$ field coordinates for $s\ge1$. A Frobenius power of an affine field-linear form is again affine in the corresponding Frobenius powers. A quadratic term with index difference in $[-s,s]$ stays in that range after substitution and trace folding. The transformed ordinary cubic contributes only additional bandwidth-one terms. A different field presentation conjugates coefficients and preserves the trace.

\section{A direct gate-program interface with charged intermediate states}\label{sec:program}
The construction can begin with an actual straight-line Boolean circuit rather than a supplied ANF. Let the circuit have $n$ original inputs, $S$ internal gates of types XOR, AND, NOT and constants, and one designated output. Wire indices give description length $|C|=O((n+S)\log(n+S+2))$ bits. The following front end is ordinary exact symbolic propagation; it is not a new circuit-equivalence algorithm.

At each wire, manufacture its complete Boolean ANF as a set of monomial masks. XOR is symmetric difference, NOT toggles the empty monomial, and AND takes all unions of two masks, canceling equal products modulo two. Multilinearity is imposed exactly through mask union. Impose an explicit term budget $M$ only \emph{after} all cancellation at a gate. Reject if the surviving ANF has more than $M$ terms. High-degree sparse intermediate states are allowed. At the final wire, verify that the actual output ANF has degree at most three and feed it to the field compiler.

\begin{proposition}[Certified program-to-field composition]
Every successful front-end execution proves its output ANF equal to the original circuit on every input. With a term budget $M$, sorting the at most $M^2$ products at each AND gives a conservative bit-time bound
\[
 O\bigl(|C|+n^2+SM^2n\log(M+2)\bigr)
\]
and storage $O(|C|+n^2+(SM+M^2)n)$ bits. The bit cost of the subsequent acquired field counter is added to this preprocessing cost. Internal wires contribute to $S$, not to the independent count $n$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Induct on topological gate order. The Boolean monomial identity $x^Ax^B=x^{A\cup B}$ makes each computed gate polynomial exact, including all cancellations. Both operands have at most $M$ terms if execution has reached the gate. Sorting and parity cancellation therefore examine at most $M^2$ masks of at most $n$ bits. All stored wire polynomials and one product list fit the stated space bound. Explicit input masks contribute $O(n^2)$ bits. The output-degree check is performed on the exact polynomial, so it is a certificate rather than a sampling assumption.
\end{proof}

The implemented default is $M=\sum_{j=0}^3\binom nj=O(n^3)$. Thus any successful gate compilation has polynomial overhead in $n+S$. The budget is charged as a numerical parameter; an arbitrarily large binary-encoded budget is not free. This is still a restricted route: an intermediate ANF can exceed the budget even if later gates cancel it completely. The circuit step neither assumes a hidden field nor supplies its coordinates to the next stage.

Two complete gate-only fixtures were executed. The 21-input circuit has 879 internal gates, including 197 ANDs; the 36-input circuit has 3,205 gates, including 578 ANDs. Their maximum intermediate ANF sizes were 852 and 4,023 respectively. They implement hidden field computations and unknown rank-two or rank-four quadratic defects without giving those descriptions to the compiler. The resulting raw ANFs matched the separately preserved raw fixtures coefficient-for-coefficient, and the acquired exact counts were $Z=128$ and $Z=-176\,128$, respectively. Each had 1,024 extra original-input gate-evaluation checks. These are actual program executions with many internal states, not timing comparisons against SAT or other competitors.

A further 886-gate, 21-input fixture contains a degree-six intermediate monomial which is mixed into the output and then cancels. The term-budget front end accepted it and the complete counter again returned $Z=128$. This repairs the unnecessarily restrictive first implementation, which rejected any high-degree intermediate. Separately, a six-input program forming $\prod_i(1+x_i)$ and then XORing it with itself was rejected at the default 42-term budget, but accepted at budget 64 with exact zero output. The failure is an honest resource boundary of this symbolic representation.

The independent gate audit checked 580 quotient-ring identities and 160 generated circuits. Its term-budget compiler accepted 150 circuits, all checked against direct gate execution on 9,600 assignments. It also accepted sparse cancellation examples with intermediate degrees 4, 8 and 20 at term budget one. Full source and exact data accompany this proof.

In the quantitative bounds below, m denotes the resulting ANF monomial count;
this is at most 2^k times the initially supplied factor count.

    Z(B,P)=sum_x (-1)^[q_B(x)+P(x)],
    q_B(x)=sum_(i<j)B_ij x_i x_j.

B may be dense and full-rank. No decomposition, sparse inverse, change of
coordinates, or short stabilizer generators are given. Define

    C_B={(a,Ba):a in F_2^n}.

Joint support weight is wt(a OR z), X weight is wt(a), and Z weight is wt(z).
These weights have different computational roles.

**Theorem.** Given support limit w and X-cost budget A_0, a deterministic
polynomial-space algorithm acquires independent a_1,...,a_r with

    wt(a_i OR Ba_i)<=w,
    A:=sum_i wt(a_i)<=A_0,
    D:=sum_i wt(Ba_i)<=rw,
    delta:=n-r.

It expresses Z(B,P) as 2^delta exactly reconstructed fixed-local phase counts,
each on N=r+2A bits, with common denominator 2^A. Each count contains at most
m+3A+D+r+O(1) monomials of degree at most max(k,2). Acquisition costs

    poly(n) 2^[O(w log(en/w))]

for 1<=w<=n/2; generally use poly(n) sum_(j<=w) binom(n,j)2^j. Total bit time is

    poly(L+n+A_0)[2^[O(w log(en/w))]
                  +2^[delta+F(N,m+3A+D+r+O(1))]],

where F is the preserved local-phase exponent with its guarded exhaustive
fallback. Space is polynomial in the explicit input and acquired certificate.

**Hidden-witness guarantee.** Suppose C_B contains an independent family of
rank n-delta_* with total X weight <=A_0 and total joint weight W_*.
The family is only an existence promise, not supplied data. Then

    delta<=delta_*+floor(W_*/(w+1)).

Therefore exact original-n counting is subexponential if

    A_0=O(n), delta_*=o(n), W_*=n exp(o(log n)),
    m=n exp(o(log n)).

Choose w=n^o(1) growing faster than W_*/n. The defect is o(n), N=O(n), and
the factor count is n exp(o(log n)). Since every nonzero a has X weight>=1,
A>=r and N>=3r=Theta(n) in this regime. Thus the phase theorem is applied at
the correct variable scale. No rank bound on B or primitive cubic block size
is required; P is arbitrary within its stated locality and density.

Budgets are search parameters, not useful representations. Unknown budgets
can be handled by acquired prefixes and a polynomial-size dovetailed portfolio.
Exhausting an unfavorable exponential case before a good one would not prove
this bound.

## 2. Weighted acquisition

For a physical support U, a graph-code word is supported in U exactly when
a_(U^c)=0 and B[U^c,U]a_U=0. Gaussian elimination obtains this kernel.
Streaming all combinations of a kernel basis enumerates all supported words.
For X weight j=1,...,w, enumerate supports of size<=w, retain kernel vectors
with wt(a)=j, and feed them into linear-matroid greedy. Every short word occurs,
possibly repeatedly, in nondecreasing X weight.

Add a word exactly when it increases rank and fits the X budget. Stop when
the next independent word exceeds that budget; all later words cost at least
as much. Each prefix has minimum X cost among independent subsets of the same
size in the searched family.

An arbitrary kernel basis alone is insufficient for this weighted claim:
it spans the directions but may not minimize X weight. The implementation
explicitly streams its combinations in the weighted routine.

Delete from the hidden witness all words of joint weight>w. At most
floor(W_*/(w+1)) are deleted. The remaining independent family has the promised
rank and X cost<=A_0, and occurs in the search. Greedy reaches at least its
rank before its budget ends. This proves the witness guarantee.

The current support, kernel, coefficient counter, independence basis and at
most n selected vectors take polynomial space. Candidate count is bounded by
poly(n) sum_(j<=w) binom(n,j)2^j; no exponential table is stored.

The simpler unweighted variant enumerates supports in increasing size and
inserts arbitrary kernel basis vectors. A newly independent vector at support
size t has actual joint weight t, since smaller directions were already
spanned. This yields the minimum-joint-weight basis prefix. If a full minimum
basis has total weight W_min, a prefix of cost W and defect delta obeys
W+delta(w+1)<=W_min. The weighted theorem is stronger for counting because
numerous Z actions add no variables.

## 3. Exact stabilizer identity, with signs

Define

    K(a)|x>=(-1)^[q_B(a)+(Ba)·x]|x+a>
           =(-1)^q_B(a) X^a Z^(Ba)|x>.

The q_B(a) sign is necessary. Quadratic polarization implies
K(a)K(b)=K(a+b). The operators commute and square to identity. For any binary
basis a_1,...,a_n,

    product_j (I+K(a_j))|0>=sum_x (-1)^q_B(x)|x>.

No normalization occurs: basis selectors parametrize every x once. This is
established stabilizer algebra, written explicitly to track phases and costs.

Complete acquired vectors to a basis with d_1,...,d_delta. For each dense
selector eta put x_eta=sum_l eta_l d_l. Applying the dense factors first gives
(-1)^q_B(x_eta)|x_eta>. The unstructured complement costs 2^delta branches
but creates no long wire trace.

## 4. Variable-efficient phase compilation and arithmetic

The conditional action of a short generator, with selector lambda_j, is

    phase (-1)^[(Ba_j)_v lambda_j y_v],
    update y_v<-y_v+(a_j)_v lambda_j,

at coordinate v, plus its global sign (-1)^[q_B(a_j)lambda_j]. At a coordinate
with both X and Z, apply the Z phase to the OLD bit before the X update.

For each X update create state bit t and multiplier mu. The exact identity

    1_[t+y_v+lambda_j=0]
       =(1/2)sum_mu (-1)^[mu(t+y_v+lambda_j)]

adds two variables and at most three quadratic or unary monomials. Z-only
actions add one local monomial and no variables. Initial wire bits are the
known x_eta. Every final physical bit is a constant or its last state bit, so
the original P factors remain k-local.

There are exactly A X updates. Hence N=r+2A and common denominator 2^A.
Summing multipliers enforces a unique trace per selector. Over eta and lambda,
the final original x runs through F_2^n exactly once, proving the identity.

Reconstruct each signed phase sum exactly, sum branch numerators, and only
then divide by 2^A. Premature division of modular residues loses precision.
A conservative numerator bound is 2^(N+delta), so O(n+A) bits suffice.
The target lies in [-2^n,2^n]; output counts are (2^n+Z)/2 and (2^n-Z)/2.
Internal states are not original independent inputs.

Once acquisition succeeds, fixed-local counting is a composition with the
governing theorem. The changed scope is the acquired interface for a raw dense
quadratic description; Fourier enforcement is established machinery.

## 5. Unknown robust sparse inverse: a concrete covered family

Suppose B=Q^(-1)+S, where Q is invertible alternating, nnz(Q)=O(n), maximum
column degree Delta=n^o(1), and S has M=n exp(o(log n)) unordered edges.
Neither Q nor S is supplied. The rows of Q form hidden independent X vectors,
whose Z rows are Q B=I+QS. Total X cost is O(n); total Z cost is at most

    n+sum_v degree_Q(v)degree_S(v)<=n+2 Delta M.

The weighted acquisition theorem applies. B can have full rank and
Theta(n^2) entries. After adding S, its inverse need not remain sparse.
No low-rank completion, repeated response types or nonlinear centroid blocks
are required. More generally, the promise is an unknown invertible multiplier
A with nnz(A)=O(n), nnz(AB)=n exp(o(log n)); an o(n)-dimensional unstructured
complement is also allowed.

An equally informed ordinary method handles the uncorrupted sparse-inverse
case directly. For nonsingular B and gamma_B=sum_x(-1)^q_B(x)=+-2^(n/2),

    Z(B,P)=2^(-n)gamma_B
       sum_(a,y)(-1)^[q_B(B^(-1)a)+a·y+P(y)].

The transformed quadratic has polar B^(-1); the displayed expression retains
its unary correction. If B^(-1) is near-linear sparse, this is a local phase
count on 2n bits. The acquired compiler adds corrupted and partial-basis cases;

## 1. Result and scope

Let the raw input be a symmetric n by n matrix B. A quadratic Boolean phase
uses its off-diagonal entries; the diagonal may be retained for algebraic
purposes. Suppose B has an unknown decomposition

\[
B=D+S,\qquad D=UKU^\top,\qquad \operatorname{rank}D=r,
\]

where U has r independent columns, K is invertible and symmetric, S is
symmetric and every row of S has at most Δ nonzero entries, including a
possible diagonal entry. Neither U, K, D, S nor a sparse graph is supplied.

Let h be a monic binary polynomial of degree q with h(S)=0. Define the
unobserved orbit matrix

\[
W=[\,U,\;SU,\;\ldots,\;S^{q-1}U\,].
\]

The class conditions are:

1. W has all qr columns independent;
2. the code spanned by W has minimum nonzero Hamming weight greater than 2Δ.

These are additional structural conditions, not consequences of arbitrary
low rank and sparsity. Their role is explicit. Crucially, the useful code
does not need to be supplied: the theorem below manufactures it directly
as the column space of h(B), and checks its decoding margin.

**Acquisition theorem.** Under these conditions, one deterministically
recovers the exact D and S from B, h and Δ in

\[
\operatorname{poly}(n+q)\,2^{qr}
\]

bit time and polynomial space. No original input coordinate is deleted,
and there is no condition involving r times the number of sparse edges.
Every returned decomposition is checked by exact matrix arithmetic.

For fixed q, h can itself be acquired by a constant-size portfolio of
all monic binary polynomials of degree at most q. For q=2 there are only
four monic quadratics, plus the two monic linear polynomials. A supplied
polynomial is therefore not an assumed decomposition.

The initial computational scope is a raw dense quadratic matrix plus
explicit fixed-locality factors in those same coordinates. The algebraic
condition h(S)=0 survives permutations and orthogonal coordinate changes.
It does not survive arbitrary congruence GSGᵀ. Consequently this result
does not automatically extend through arbitrary GL block gauges from the
cubic centroid compiler. No unknown metric is being assumed.

## 2. Why the raw polynomial h(B) reveals the code

**Lemma.** If W has full column rank, then

\[
h(B)=WHW^\top
\]

for an invertible symmetric qr by qr matrix H. In q by q blocks of size r,

\[
H_{ij}=0\quad(i+j>q-1),\qquad
H_{ij}=K\quad(i+j=q-1),
\]

where block indices run from zero to q−1. Therefore

\[
\operatorname{rank}h(B)=qr,\qquad
\operatorname{im}h(B)=\operatorname{im}W.
\]

**Proof.** Expand each power of B=S+D as a sum of noncommutative words.
The terms containing no D sum to h(S)=0. In every remaining word, write
the segment before the first D as S^i and the segment after the last D
as S^j. Substitution D=UKUᵀ factors that word as

\[
S^iU\,H_{ij}^{(\mathrm{word})}\,U^\top S^j.
\]

Its outer exponents satisfy i+j≤q−1. Equality is possible only for the
single-D terms of the leading power B^q, because h is monic. Every such
term is S^i U K Uᵀ S^j with i+j=q−1. Thus the asserted zero pattern and
anti-diagonal blocks follow.

The polynomial h(B) is symmetric. Since W has full column rank, its core
H in a factorization WHWᵀ is unique, so H is symmetric. Reverse the
block columns of H: the resulting matrix is block triangular with
invertible diagonal blocks K. Hence H is invertible. Finally W is
injective and Wᵀ is surjective, so WHWᵀ has rank qr and image im W.
This proves the lemma.

For a quadratic h(t)=t²+a t+b, the identity is especially explicit:

\[
h(B)=[U,SU]
\begin{bmatrix} K(U^\top U)K+aK&K\\ K&0\end{bmatrix}
[U,SU]^\top,
\]

Equivalently,

\[
h(B)=U[K(U^\top U)K+aK]U^\top
      +UKU^\top S+SUKU^\top.
\]

The block core is invertible whenever K is. This does not rely on a real or complex
eigendecomposition, spectral gap, incoherence oracle, or a known sparse
matrix.

## 3. Raw algorithm and exact certification

Compute h(B) by matrix polynomial evaluation and find a full-column-rank
basis V of its image by binary elimination. On the promised family V
has d=qr columns, although neither U nor W has been given.

Stream all 2^d codewords of im V using Gray-code enumeration. Find the
minimum nonzero Hamming weight. Reject this route if it is at most 2Δ.
For every observed column B_j, stream the codewords again and find a
codeword D'_j satisfying

\[
\operatorname{wt}(B_j-D'_j)\le\Delta.
\]

There is at most one, because two such codewords would differ by a
nonzero codeword of weight at most 2Δ. Under the theorem's hypotheses
the true D_j belongs to im U⊆im V, while B_j-D_j=S_j has weight at most
Δ. Therefore D'_j exists and equals D_j.

Assemble D', set S'=B-D', and verify:

- exact entrywise equality;
- symmetry of D' and S';
- the rank of D';
- the row-weight and off-diagonal edge budgets;
- h(S')=0.

The promised family recovers exactly its D and S. Outside that family,
any accepted output is still an exact, independently checked
representation; failed hypotheses cannot cause an incorrect count.

Matrix polynomial evaluation costs O(qn³) elementary binary operations
by ordinary multiplication. Rank and symmetry checks are polynomial.
The distance computation and n decodings cost O(n² 2^d) bit operations
with a conservative accounting, and all codewords can be streamed.
Storage is O(n²+nd+q) bits apart from polynomial indexing overhead;
there is no exponential codeword table.

If the annihilating polynomial is not supplied, enumerate the monic
polynomials through a degree budget q₀, compute each raw image rank
first, and discard images above a chosen code-dimension budget d₀.
The total acquisition bound is

\[
2^{q_0+1}\operatorname{poly}(n+q_0)\,2^{d_0}.
\]

Whenever a promised polynomial has degree q≤q₀ and qr≤d₀, its trial
succeeds. Degree and dimension budgets may be dovetailed by their
explicit work bound. Running an unfavorable full-rank code trial to
completion before trying a good polynomial would not justify the
promised complexity.

The implementation takes h and Δ as explicit trial parameters. These
are small integer/model budgets, not hidden matrix data.

## 4. Original-input exact counting

Consider the explicitly described phase sum

\[
Z=\sum_{x\in\mathbb F_2^n}
(-1)^{q_{\mathrm{off}(B)}(x)}
\prod_{j=1}^{m}\phi_j(x|_{A_j}),
\]

Every A_j has fixed size at most k and each local phase has a fixed
power-of-two root order. The input length L includes the raw n by n
quadratic matrix and every local factor; generally L is at least of
order n². The variable count is the original n.

After acquisition, let M=e(S) be its explicitly counted number of
off-diagonal edges. The residual contributes exactly M quadratic
factors, with M≤nΔ/2. The recovered symmetric D has rank r.
Use the preserved exact quadratic refinement and Gaussian-Walsh
expansion of its rank-r core. There are at most 2^r characters, and
every character changes only original-variable unary phases.

For a symmetric core K the fourth-root refinement includes the known
unary diagonal and Boolean substitution corrections; dropping these
corrections is invalid. Each inner local-phase answer is reconstructed
exactly before Gaussian multiplication and division by the Fourier
denominator. The numerator has O(n+r) bits in a fixed-dimensional
cyclotomic integer basis.

Writing F(n,m') for the preserved local-phase exponent, the complete
conditional bit bound is

\[
\operatorname{poly}(L+n+q)
\left(2^{qr}+2^{\,r+F(n,m+M+O(n))}\right).
\]

This is poly(L+n+q)2^o(n) with polynomial space when
